content: 1. One study (den Boon, 2006) demonstrated a high risk of selection bias, while two other studies had an unclear risk of bias regarding the reference standard. In 9 out of 11 studies, fewer than half of the participants underwent the reference standard test. Accuracy calculations assumed that participants who did not receive the reference standard were cultureand/or smear-negative, indicating no active tuberculosis (TB). 2. There were no significant concerns about the applicability of the evidence, as assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. 3. Moderate heterogeneity was observed in sensitivity estimates, while specificity estimates showed significant heterogeneity based on visual inspection of confidence intervals (CIs). This led to a downgrading of specificity. 4. Sensitivity estimates were precise, but specificity estimates were imprecise, leading to concerns about the reliability of specificity data. 5. Publication bias was not formally assessed due to limited evidence available for diagnostic test accuracy studies. However, it is generally considered unlikely to affect the conclusions. 6. The GRADE profile tables for new recommendations on latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) management were updated and consolidated. These guidelines evaluated whether interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) could serve as an alternative to tuberculin skin tests (TSTs) in identifying individuals at high risk of progressing from LTBI to active TB in high-incidence settings. 7. Longitudinal studies on the predictive value of positive IGRA results in high TB-incidence countries (≥100/100,000) are still emerging. These studies should ideally include follow-up periods of at least one year, either active or passive, and account for factors such as HIV status and Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination. 8. The overall quality of evidence for TST and IGRA was rated as very low due to serious risks of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. For example, TST showed an additional 10 cases per 1,000 (ranging from 4 fewer to 37 more), while IGRA showed 15 more cases per 1,000 (ranging from 3 more to 36 more). 9. Subgroup analyses, such as progression to active TB among healthcare workers, revealed serious risks of bias and imprecision. For instance, one study reported 6 fewer cases per 1,000 for TST (ranging from 9 fewer to 82 more), but no computable difference for IGRA. 10. The quality of evidence for preventive treatment options, such as 3-month daily rifampicin plus isoniazid (3RH) for children and adolescents under 15 years, was rated as low. The effect estimates showed 60 more cases per 1,000 (ranging from 9 more to 121 more). 11. For adults with HIV, 3-month weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid (3HP) was compared to 6 or 9 months of isoniazid monotherapy. The overall quality of evidence was high, with 44 fewer cases per 1,000 (ranging from 26 fewer to 52 fewer). However, open-label trial designs may have introduced ascertainment bias. 12. For adults without HIV, the quality of evidence for 3HP was moderate. The effect estimates showed 0 fewer cases per 1,000 (ranging from 1 fewer to 2 more), with some concerns about imprecision and the lack of comparison with 6-month isoniazid. 13. Preventive treatment for contacts of patients with multidrug-resistant (MDR) or rifampicin-resistant TB was assessed. The overall quality of evidence was very low due to small sample sizes, wide CIs, and risks of bias in the selection of control groups. No evidence was available for mortality, adverse events, or the development of drug resistance. 14. Across studies, risks of bias included selection bias, incorporation bias, and publication bias. Many studies did not use microbiological tools to confirm TB diagnoses, and large prospective studies remain unpublished or ongoing. 15. The GRADE assessment consistently downgraded evidence due to serious risks of bias, unexplained inconsistencies, and imprecision in effect estimates. For example, wide CIs often indicated both significant predictive performance and a lack of predictive utility. 16. The analysis highlighted the need for more robust, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and larger sample sizes to improve the reliability of evidence for LTBI management and TB prevention strategies.
